questions.stem: Which list names all four kinds of pyrotechnic distress signal in the Small Vessel Regulations?
options: Rocket parachute flare, multi-star flare, hand flare, and buoyant or hand smoke signal
Rocket parachute flare, red lamp, hand flare, and whistle
Orange smoke, torch, signal mirror, and rocket parachute flare
Multi-star flare, hand flare, strobe light, and flag
questions.explanation: Section 1 of the SVR defines a pyrotechnic distress signal as a rocket parachute flare, a multi-star flare, a hand flare, or a buoyant or hand smoke signal. Mirrors, lamps, flags and whistles are not pyrotechnic distress signals.

questions.stem: A required flare was made on 1 March 2022. On which date does it expire under the Small Vessel Regulations?
options: 1 March 2026
1 March 2024
1 March 2027
The date it was bought plus four years
questions.explanation: A required pyrotechnic distress signal expires four years after its date of manufacture, so 1 March 2022 plus four years is 1 March 2026. The count starts at manufacture, not purchase.

questions.stem: A passenger-carrying vessel of 10 m under SVR Part 4 (not more than 15 gross tonnage, 12 passengers or fewer) is checked for visual signals. What must she carry?
options: A watertight flashlight and twelve pyrotechnic distress signals, not more than six of them smoke signals
A watertight flashlight and six pyrotechnic distress signals, none of them smoke
Three pyrotechnic distress signals only
Twelve smoke signals and no flares
questions.explanation: Section 410 gives, for a vessel of more than 9 m, a watertight flashlight and twelve pyrotechnic distress signals of which not more than six are smoke signals. Six non-smoke signals applies to 6 m up to 9 m, and three to a vessel of 6 m or less.

questions.stem: In which frequency band do an EPIRB and a PLB operate under the Navigation Safety Regulations, 2020?
options: The 406 MHz band
The 121.5 MHz band
9 GHz
156.8 MHz (VHF channel 16)
questions.explanation: The regulations define both as operating in the 406 MHz band, which is the band Cospas-Sarsat satellites detect. 9 GHz is the SART's radar band, and VHF channel 16 is a voice channel.

questions.stem: The vessel is sold and the contact details of her EPIRB registration change. Within what time must the Canadian Beacon Registry be updated?
options: 30 days after the change
7 days after the change
6 months after the change
Only at the next annual inspection
questions.explanation: Section 228(2) requires the registration to be updated within 30 days after a change. Six months is the interval for inspecting and testing the beacon, a different rule.

questions.stem: Which statement about a float-free EPIRB under s. 209 of the Navigation Safety Regulations, 2020 is correct?
options: It is required on a near coastal Class 1 or unlimited voyage; it must float free if the vessel sinks, be readily accessible near the navigating position unless remotely activated, and be able to be released by hand and carried into a survival craft
It is required only on vessels over 150 gross tonnage and must be bolted to the mast
It is required on every vessel, and it must be kept locked in the master's cabin
It is required only in sheltered waters and must be stowed below deck
questions.explanation: Section 209(1) requires a float-free EPIRB on a vessel on a near coastal voyage Class 1 or an unlimited voyage (and on a vessel over 12 m on an inland or near coastal Class 2 voyage), and s. 209(2) requires it to float free, be readily accessible near the navigating position unless it can be activated remotely, and be released by hand and carried into a survival craft. The other options invent a tonnage test or put the beacon where it cannot work.

questions.stem: A 10 m vessel on a near coastal voyage, Class 2 carries a manually activated EPIRB. Where should it be?
options: Worn by the person in charge of the navigational watch or stowed so it is readily accessible for immediate use if the vessel is abandoned
Locked in the master's cabin
Fixed to the mast and never removed
Stored with the spare flares in a sealed box below
questions.explanation: Section 209(4) says a manually activated EPIRB, a PLB or a DSC handheld must be worn by the person in charge of the navigational watch or, if that is not practicable, stowed so it is readily accessible for immediate use. A locked or buried beacon cannot be grabbed in an emergency.

questions.stem: Which statement about EPIRB testing and maintenance is correct?
options: EPIRBs, PLBs and SARTs are inspected and tested by a radio operator at least every six months; the EPIRB release mechanism is replaced on or before its marked date; the battery is replaced after an inadvertent activation
Beacons are tested every year; the release mechanism is never replaced; the battery is replaced only when it fails
Beacons are tested every three months by any crew member; the battery is never replaced
Beacons are tested every two years; the release mechanism and battery are replaced only at expiry
questions.explanation: Section 239 requires inspection and testing by a radio operator on installation and at least every six months. Section 230 requires the release mechanism to be replaced on or before its marked replacement date, and the EPIRB or PLB battery to be replaced after use in an emergency, after inadvertent activation, after a test requires it, and by its expiry date. A SART battery is replaced by its expiry date (s. 231).

questions.stem: Which statement about a radar SART is correct?
options: It answers 9 GHz (X-band) radar only, and shows as a line of 12 dots that become arcs and then full circles within about 1 nautical mile
It answers 3 GHz radar only, and shows as a single flashing echo
It answers VHF radio calls and shows the vessel's name on the chart plotter
It answers 406 MHz satellites and shows as a line of 3 dots
questions.explanation: A radar SART replies to 9 GHz (X-band) radar with a line of 12 dots, which become arcs and then full circles when the rescuer is within about 1 nautical mile. It does not answer 3 GHz radar, and 406 MHz is the band of EPIRBs and PLBs, not the SART's radar reply.

questions.stem: Scenario: a crew member knocks the EPIRB switch and it starts transmitting. What should the OOW do?
options: Switch it from ON to ARMED/SAFE and contact the Canadian Mission Control Centre to report the false alert
Leave it on until the battery runs out
Throw it overboard so it stops transmitting
Wait for the Coast Guard to call, then explain
questions.explanation: The Canadian Coast Guard Notice to Mariners says to switch the beacon off its ON position and contact the Canadian Mission Control Centre. Leaving it on or throwing it overboard keeps a false alert running, and waiting for a call delays resolution. The battery is also replaced afterwards.
